workload.description: Low request rate, very long jobs: the runner fleet is the whole system

components.name: API gateway (webhooks, status API, artifact URLs)
PostgreSQL (runs, jobs, logs index, run state)

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: db.t4g.medium — AWS RDS PostgreSQL us-east-1 / On-Demand / Single-AZ (band high = Multi-AZ) / 730 h per month; INSTANCE-HOURS ONLY (excludes storage, provisioned IOPS and backup above the free allocation). Band: deployment spread: low = Single-AZ, high = Multi-AZ. Both are on-demand, standard-tier, us-east-1 PostgreSQL, so the band is fully in scope. Multi-AZ is ~2x Single-AZ.

citations.note: $0.065/h Single-AZ x 730 = 4745c/month. MySQL/MariaDB run ~3.9% cheaper than PostgreSQL for the same class.

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: kafka.t3.small — AWS MSK us-east-1 / On-Demand / provisioned broker / 730 h per month; broker-hour only (excludes storage and data transfer). Band: zero-width: single published broker-hour rate in the pinned scope.

components.name: Build runner fleet (one job per runner at a time)

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: c6g.large — AWS EC2 us-east-1 / On-Demand / Linux / shared tenancy / 730 h per month; instance-hour only (excludes EBS, data transfer); arm64 (Graviton2). Band: zero-width: within the pinned scope the hourly list rate is a single exact published number with no variance. Month length (672-744 h), burstable credit surcharges, Savings Plans and Spot are OUT-OF-BAND modifiers, named per row, not band edges.

citations.note: $0.068/h x 730 = 4964c/month. Cross-checked to the cent against the AWS Price List Bulk API (version 20260904231117).

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 6 req/s peak - CI is a LOW-request, HIGH-work system. Mix: 55% status/badge polling, 25% artifact and cache I/O, 12% log tailing, 8% build triggers (~0.48 builds/s peak, ~14,000 builds/day at average load)

assumptions.subject: runner
assumptions.statement: A runner executes ONE job at a time and the average job takes 5 minutes, so a runner's capacity is 1/300 = 0.0033 jobs/s. Its base_latency_ms is 300,000 - a build really does take five minutes, and the engine is being told the truth rather than a number that looks like a web request. 190 runners hold ~0.48 builds/s at 76% utilisation

assumptions.subject: runner
assumptions.statement: The fleet is sized for PEAK and billed 24/7 at on-demand list price, because the engine models neither autoscaling nor spot. A real fleet scales toward zero off-peak and runs interruptible instances; both together cut this line by roughly 75-85%. Read ~$9.4k/month as the honest ceiling for a statically-provisioned fleet, not as what you would pay

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Everything except the runners sits near 0% utilisation, and that is the correct answer, not a modelling error: the request tier of a CI system is trivial. Sizing here is driven by job DURATION, not by request rate

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: 3 brokers for quorum/HA. At ~0.5 jobs/s the queue is effectively idle; it exists for durability of dispatch, not throughput

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The SQL primary is modelled as ONE instance because there is one writer. A Multi-AZ standby is assumed in a real deployment but is NOT modelled as a second instance: it serves no traffic, and the engine would credit it with capacity it does not have. The engine will therefore flag the primary as a single point of failure - that flag is correct about failover, not about capacity.

assumptions.subject: store
assumptions.statement: 40 TB: artifacts, dependency caches and logs with a ~30-day retention

assumptions.subject: pricing
assumptions.statement: Monthly usage volumes (egress/storage/requests) are derived from AVERAGE load = peak / 3; capacity and instance counts are sized to PEAK. A single system_rps cannot carry both, so the peak:average ratio is stated here rather than hidden in a volume.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: LATENCY FOR THE BUILD FLOW IS WRONG AND WE KNOW WHY. The engine's per-component sojourn time is an M/M/1 form, service_time / (1 - rho), applied to the fleet's AGGREGATE utilisation. With one server that is right; with 190 servers at 76% it is not - Erlang-C says a job almost never waits, yet the engine inflates a 300-second build to a ~3,700-second p95 (~12x). Read the runner's 76% utilisation and the capacity headroom, which ARE correct; ignore the push_build flow's latency figure. The headline latency of this design is unaffected: the dominant flow is status polling (55% of requests, ~21 ms), which touches no runner.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: What a CI user actually feels is queue WAIT on a bursty morning-commit spike. The engine models steady-state arrivals, not backlog: it will not tell you how deep the job queue gets at 09:05 or how long it takes to drain. Treat 76% as headroom, not as a promise about wait time.

_library.summary: Webhook-triggered build pipeline where a long-job runner fleet, not request rate, sets the capacity.
